"Entirety" means the complete whole of something — every single part of it, with nothing left out, nothing removed, and nothing divided. It is not a partial amount, not most of it, not almost all of it — it is every bit of it, fully and completely.

A simple image to anchor this: if you have a pizza with 8 slices, the entirety of that pizza is all 8 slices as one complete, undivided thing — not 7, not 6, but all of them together.
The Most Common Phrase: "In Its Entirety"

The phrase "in its entirety" is where you will encounter this word most often. It means "as a complete whole" or "completely, with nothing left out."

"I watched the movie in its entirety."
→ The whole movie was watched — from the very first scene to the very last. Not an excerpt, not most of it — all of it.

"The company was sold in its entirety."
→ The entire company was sold as one complete unit — every department, every asset, every employee. Nothing was split off or held back.

"Please read the contract in its entirety before signing."
→ Read every single word — don't skim, don't skip any section, don't stop halfway.
The Other Common Structure: "The Entirety Of..."

You will also see "the entirety of [something]," which means "the whole of something" — all of it, without exception.

"The entirety of his savings was spent on the trip."
→ Every single penny he had saved — all of it — was spent. Not a portion of it.

"She devoted the entirety of her career to helping others."
→ Her whole career, from the very first day to the very last, was dedicated to that cause. Not just one phase of it — all of it.

"The entirety of the audience stood and applauded."
→ Every single person in the room stood up. Nobody stayed seated.
The Special Power of This Word

Here is the most important thing to understand: "entirety" does not simply mean "all." Its real job is to deliberately draw your attention to the fact that nothing has been left out, cut short, or divided. It is a word of strong, conscious emphasis on completeness.

Compare these two sentences:

"I read the report." → Neutral. You read it.
"I read the report in its entirety." → Emphatic. You are making the specific point that you read every single word — nothing was skipped or glossed over.

Writers and speakers reach for "entirety" when they want the listener to understand with full clarity: this is the whole thing, not a fraction of it. That deliberate emphasis on wholeness is the defining personality of the word.

You will encounter this word in legal language ("the debt must be paid in its entirety"), in formal writing ("the committee reviewed the proposal in its entirety"), in journalism ("the speech was broadcast in its entirety"), and occasionally in emphatic everyday speech ("I can't believe I ate the entire cake in its entirety!").

It is a moderately formal word. In casual conversation, people tend to just say "the whole thing" or "all of it." But in professional, legal, and written contexts, "entirety" is very common.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Whole is the simpler, everyday version of the same idea — "the whole story," "the whole team." "Entirety" is more formal and carries more deliberate emphasis on completeness.

Totality is a close cousin but tends to be used for large, abstract ideas — "the totality of human knowledge," "the totality of the evidence." "Entirety" feels more concrete and is more common in everyday formal writing.

Completeness is subtly different: it refers to the quality of being complete ("the completeness of the data"), whereas "entirety" refers to the whole thing itself ("the entirety of the data").

Entirety = the complete, undivided whole of something — every part included, nothing left out. Most commonly appears as "in its entirety" (meaning: completely, as a whole, with nothing omitted) and "the entirety of..." (meaning: the whole of something).
